The three notebooks below accompany Unit 1. They are ordinary Jupyter
notebooks and need only `numpy` (plus `matplotlib` for the plots); open
them in JupyterLab, VS Code, or any notebook environment.

## The dynamic programming algorithm

A general implementation of the dynamic programming algorithm for
deterministic finite-horizon problems with finite state and input spaces
-- exactly the setting of the transition diagrams in the notes. The
problem is supplied as the transition map and the arc costs, and the
routine returns the costs-to-go $J_k$ together with *all* minimizing
decisions at each state, so the non-uniqueness discussed in the notes is
visible directly in the output. The other two notebooks build on this
routine.

[Download `A_1_dp.ipynb`](A_1_dp.ipynb){download="A_1_dp.ipynb"}

## Inventory control

The inventory control example worked through in the notes: a shop decides
how many items of a product to order at each stage, with the stock
evolving as $x_{k+1}=\max\{x_k+u_k-d_k,0\}$ under a known demand, over a
finite horizon. The notebook sets the problem up in the form expected by
the dynamic programming routine above and recovers the costs-to-go and
the optimal ordering policy.

[Download `A_1_inventorycontrol.ipynb`](A_1_inventorycontrol.ipynb){download="A_1_inventorycontrol.ipynb"}

## Angle estimation with the Viterbi algorithm

An application of dynamic programming to *estimation* rather than
control: recovering the angle of a spinning wheel from noisy hue
measurements produced by a camera. The angle is quantized into $N$
values, so the problem is that of finding the most likely state sequence
of a hidden Markov chain given the measurements -- which, after taking
logarithms, is again a shortest-path problem solved by the dynamic
programming algorithm. This is the Viterbi algorithm.

[Download `A_1_A_Viterbi.ipynb`](A_1_A_Viterbi.ipynb){download="A_1_A_Viterbi.ipynb"}
